title: Beware of UPI Scams
summary: Learn to spot common scams that trick people into sending money using UPI. Always remember that you never need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money.

sections.heading: The 'Receive Money' Trick
sections.body: Scammers might send you a UPI 'collect request' pretending it's for a payment you're supposed to receive. They'll ask you to enter your UPI PIN to 'confirm' the receipt. This is a scam! Your UPI PIN is only used to send money, never to receive it.

sections.heading: Urgency and Fake Links
sections.body: Be wary of messages that create urgency, like 'your account will be blocked' or 'update your KYC now'. These often contain fake links that look real. Banks will usually ask you to visit a branch or use their official app for such tasks, not click on a link in an SMS.

sections.heading: Fake Job Offers and Digital Arrests
sections.body: Scammers might offer easy money for simple tasks like liking videos, asking for a small registration fee. They might also falsely claim you're in 'digital arrest' and need to transfer money for verification. Remember, police never ask you to transfer money, and paying to get a job is a major red flag.

example.title: Rohan and the Fake Sofa Sale
example.body: Rohan decided to sell his old sofa online. A buyer messaged him, saying they wanted to pay ₹4,999 via UPI. The buyer then sent Rohan a UPI 'collect request' for ₹4,999, with a note saying 'Payment for sofa'. The request asked Rohan to enter his UPI PIN to 'receive' the money. Rohan almost entered his PIN, but then remembered a friend's warning about this scam. He realised he never needs a PIN to receive money and ignored the request, saving himself from losing ₹4,999.

takeaway: Never share your UPI PIN or OTP with anyone, and always be suspicious of messages demanding urgent action or asking you to enter your PIN to receive money.
